## #1 Generalized Images for Brownian First Passage to Monomial Boundaries [PDF] [Copy] [Kimi] [REL]

We study the first passage of Brownian motion to a monomial moving boundary. For every integer degree at least two, we construct a time-independent signed image measure whose heat potential is the killed Brownian transition density on a nonzero interval of the natural Brownian time scale. The image density is determined by a second-kind Volterra equation in the image coordinate, not by the classical Volterra equations in time for the hitting density. Its kernel is an explicit Wright function, and the first-passage density is recovered afterwards from the boundary flux. Exponential bounds establish convergence, while a beta-moment transform connects the Wright kernel with the finite-order differential hierarchy previously obtained from transported moving zeros. A cubic numerical experiment independently checks the resulting density against simulated Brownian paths.

## Tao Tang ∗ Xiang Xu † Jin Cheng ‡

Abstract 

The main purpose of this work is to provide a novel numerical approach for the Volterra integral equations based on a spectral approach. keenable.snippet:
The paper tackles a classic problem in probability theory: figuring out how long it takes for a randomly wandering particle (Brownian motion) to first reach a moving boundary. Specifically, the boundary moves according to a power law in time, like a parabola or a cubic curve.

The main contribution is a new mathematical construction called a "generalized image measure." The classical approach to solving heat flow problems near boundaries uses the method of images, where you place a fictional mirror source of heat on the other side of a wall to enforce the right boundary condition. Here, the boundary is moving and curved, so the authors generalize this idea into something more flexible: a signed measure (meaning it can have both positive and negative parts) that is fixed in time but spread across a spatial coordinate. They show this object satisfies an equation of a specific type (a Volterra equation of the second kind) whose building block is a special mathematical function called a Wright function. Once they find this image measure, they can extract the actual first-passage probability density by tracking the flux of probability at the boundary.

The M-Wright function as a generalization of the Gaussian density for fractional diffusion processes
Abstract

The leading role of a special function of the Wright-type, referred to as M-Wright or Mainardi function, within a parametric class of self-similar stochastic processes with stationary increments, is surveyed. This class of processes, known as generalized grey Brownian motion, provides models for both fast and slow anomalous diffusion. In view of a subordination-type formula involving M-Wright functions, these processes emerge to have all finite moments and be uniquely defined by their mean and auto-covariance structure like Gaussian processes. The corresponding master equation is shown to be a fractional differential equation in the Erdélyi-Kober sense and the diffusive process is named Erdélyi-Kober fractional diffusion. In Appendix, an historical overview on the M-Wright function is reported.

parallel.title: The Wright function – hypergeometric representation and symbolical evaluation
parallel.snippet: The Wright function, which arises in the theory of the space-time fractional diffusion equation, is an interesting mathematical object which has diverse connections with other special and elementary functions. The Wright function provides a unified treatment of several classes of special functions, such as the Gaussian, Airy, Bessel, and Error functions, etc. The manuscript demonstrates an algorithm for symbolical representation in terms of finite sums of hypergeometric (HG) functions and polynomials. The HG functions are then represented by known elementary or other special functions, wherever possible. The algorithm is programmed in the open-source computer algebra system Maxima and can be used to for testing numerical algorithms for the evaluation of the Wright function.

## Abstract

The first passage time (FPT) problem for Brownian motion has been extensively studied in the literature. In particular, many incarnations of integral equations which link the density of the hitting time to the equation for the boundary itself have appeared. Most interestingly, Peskir (2002b) demonstrates that a master integral equation can be used to generate a countable number of new integrals via its differentiation or integration. In this thesis, we generalize Peskir's results and provide a more powerful unifying framework for generating integral equations through a new class of martingales. We obtain a continuum of new Volterra type equations and prove uniqueness for a subclass. The uniqueness result is then employed to demonstrate how certain functional transforms of the boundary affect the density function. Furthermore, we generalize a class of Fredholm integral equations and show its fundamental connection to the new class of Volterra equations. ## Abstract

In this work, delay stochastic fractional reaction-diffusion equations driven by standard Brownian motion and fractional Brownian motion are considered. ultimate.snippet: We study the first passage of Brownian motion to a monomial moving boundary. For every integer degree at least two, we construct a time-independent signed image measure whose heat potential is the killed Brownian transition density on a nonzero interval of the natural Brownian time scale. The image density is determined by a second-kind Volterra equation in the image coordinate, not by the classical Volterra equations in time for the hitting density. Its kernel is an explicit Wright function, and the first-passage density is recovered afterwards from the boundary flux. Exponential bounds establish convergence, while a beta-moment transform connects the Wright kernel with the finite-order differential hierarchy previously obtained from transported moving zeros. A cubic numerical experiment independently checks the resulting density against simulated Brownian paths.

The paper tackles a classic problem in probability theory: figuring out how long it takes for a randomly wandering particle (Brownian motion) to first reach a moving boundary. Specifically, the boundary moves according to a power law in time, like a parabola or a cubic curve.

The main contribution is a new mathematical construction called a "generalized image measure." The classical approach to solving heat flow problems near boundaries uses the method of images, where you place a fictional mirror source of heat on the other side of a wall to enforce the right boundary condition. Here, the boundary is moving and curved, so the authors generalize this idea into something more flexible: a signed measure (meaning it can have both positive and negative parts) that is fixed in time but spread across a spatial coordinate. They show this object satisfies an equation of a specific type (a Volterra equation of the second kind) whose building block is a special mathematical function called a Wright function. Once they find this image measure, they can extract the actual first-passage probability density by tracking the flux of probability at the boundary.
